title: Food delivery apps and the restaurants on them

turns.speaker: Sol
turns.text: The place on the corner has come off all the apps. The owner said the commission was around thirty per cent.

turns.speaker: Patrick
turns.text: Thirty per cent of a meal with maybe a ten per cent margin. That's not a partnership, that's the whole profit and more.

turns.speaker: Nia
turns.text: The defence is that it's incremental orders they wouldn't have had. Which is true at first and stops being true.

turns.speaker: Nia
turns.text: Once enough people order by app, the walk-in customer becomes an app customer. You're paying commission on the person who used to come in.

turns.speaker: Patrick
turns.text: And you can't leave, because your competitor is still on it and the app owns the habit.

turns.speaker: Nia
turns.text: That's the trap precisely. It isn't a channel any more, it's the market.

turns.speaker: Sol
turns.text: Some places just raise app prices to cover it.

turns.speaker: Patrick
turns.text: Most contracts forbid that, or did until regulators started looking.

turns.speaker: Nia
turns.text: The riders are the other half and they're paid per delivery, so the waiting isn't paid at all.

turns.speaker: Sol
turns.text: Is there a version of this that works for anyone but the app?

turns.speaker: Patrick
turns.text: The co-operative ones in a few cities charge maybe five per cent and hand the rest over. They stay small because they can't fund the discounts.

turns.speaker: Nia
turns.text: Which is the pattern everywhere. The better model loses on marketing spend rather than on merit.

points: A restaurant left delivery apps over commission of around thirty per cent, against margins near ten per cent.
Nia explains the incremental-orders defence holds initially but fails as walk-in customers convert to app customers.
Restaurants cannot leave because competitors remain and the app owns customer habit, making it the market rather than a channel.
Contracts have typically prevented charging higher prices on apps, until regulatory attention.
Riders are paid per delivery, so waiting time is unpaid.
Co-operative alternatives charging around five per cent exist but stay small because they cannot fund discounts, so the better model loses on marketing rather than merit.
